title: Children Helped Make the Middle East's Oldest Clay Figures
summary:
Thousands of years before anyone invented pottery, people in the Middle East were already shaping clay into tiny figures. Now archaeologists say more than 150 of these miniature artworks, found at sites across present-day Israel, are likely the earliest clay figures ever found in the region. And some of them were made by children.

The figures date back 11,500 to 15,000 years. They were made by the Natufians, a people who lived in the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE. The Natufians were hunter-gatherers who were beginning to settle down and move toward farming, long before the first permanent villages appeared in the region.

The figures show animals such as birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as male and female people. Some still carry traces of pigment and dyes. Others carry something even more personal: the ancient fingerprints of the artists who made them.

Those fingerprints tell a surprising story. By studying the marks left in the clay, researchers found that both children and adults took part in making the figures.

That matters because clay is not like stone or bone. Earlier Natufian figures were carved from hard materials by breaking, sanding, or whittling them into shape. Clay demanded different skills: shaping soft earth, then baking and hardening it into something that would last. As the study's authors wrote, the shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge.

The findings were published in the journal PLOS One. Laurent Davin, a study co-author and archaeologist at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said people were already using clay to create figures thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world. What fascinates him most, he said, is the evidence that children helped make these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations.
why_it_matters: The figures show that creativity and shared knowledge crossed generations thousands of years before farming and pottery, and they push back the story of how people first learned to work with clay.

background_read: Archaeologists study objects left behind by people long ago to learn how they lived, what they believed, and how they made things.
Clay is soft earth that can be shaped by hand and then baked hard, which is why people later used it to make pots and other useful objects.
The Natufians lived at a turning point in history, when people were starting to settle in one place and grow food instead of moving around to find it.
Fingerprints left in soft clay can survive for a very long time once the clay hardens, giving a direct link to the people who made an object.
